corrections.text: The Overview says Aikido reports that a threat actor pushed a malicious workflow payload "into tens of thousands of repositories". That is Aikido's wording, but the counts differ by what is measured: the 61,764 repositories Aikido counts are those that received probe pull requests, while the cited counts of repositories where the stealer was pushed or ran are lower. StepSecurity says the stealer was pushed only where permissions let it run, "thousands of repositories rather than all 63,000", and The Hacker News reports SafeDep counting 8,093 public repositories with malicious commits on default branches. Aikido has indications that the payload ran in at least 1,806 repositories.

The article sets Aikido's 61,764 repositories (the unit is repositories, not pull requests) beside StepSecurity's more than 63,000 probe pull requests. Aikido's page also gives a pull-request figure: GitHub search returned 61,839 "docs: dependency audit notes" pull requests opened between 12:45 UTC on November 10 and 15:00 UTC on November 11. StepSecurity's 63,000 is a GitHub search result at 07:40 UTC on November 12, so the two pull-request counts cover different cut-off times.

The article says StepSecurity "describes a Nextcloud run that survived until a developer reverted the commit 27 minutes later". StepSecurity says the stealer ran in nextcloud/docker three seconds after the commit, the run was never deleted, and a Nextcloud developer, not the attacker, reverted the commit 27 minutes later. The 27-minute interval is therefore an example of the cleanup failing, not of the attacker's own revert taking that long.
